questions.q: You set `APP_ENV=production` without export, then run a script with `./deploy.sh`. What does the script see when it reads $APP_ENV?
options: staging, the default value
An error, because unexported variables are illegal
production, same as the parent shell
Nothing — the variable wasn't exported, so the child process doesn't inherit it
questions.explain: A plain assignment only exists in the current shell. Without export, a child process launched from that shell does not inherit the variable.

options: A single directory where all commands must be installed
A variable that stores your current working directory
A colon-separated list of directories the shell searches, in order, for a typed command name
A list of all environment variables currently set
questions.explain: PATH is searched left to right; the first directory in the list containing a matching executable is the one used.

options: The contents of the deploy-tool script
A list of every directory on PATH
Whether deploy-tool is currently running as a process
The full path to the executable that running `deploy-tool` would actually use
questions.explain: which searches PATH and reports the full path of the executable that would run, which is useful for confirming exactly which version of a command is in effect.

questions.q: Why would you prepend a directory to PATH, like `export PATH="/opt/northbridge/bin:$PATH"`, rather than append it?
options: Prepending removes all other directories from PATH
Prepending makes the shell check that directory first, so a custom tool there takes priority over a system command of the same name
It has no effect either way
Appending is not valid syntax
questions.explain: PATH is searched in order from left to right, so prepending a directory gives it priority over directories that come after it.

questions.q: You add `export APP_ENV=production` to `~/.bashrc`. Why do you also need to run `source ~/.bashrc` (or open a new shell)?
options: .bashrc changes require a full system reboot
source deletes the old value of APP_ENV
Editing .bashrc automatically applies to all open shells immediately
~/.bashrc only runs when a new shell starts, or when you explicitly re-run it with source
questions.explain: ~/.bashrc is read when a shell starts. An already-running shell won't pick up the change until you source the file again or open a new terminal.
